#4124. Battlefield 6’s first big map in months is coming to Labs soon, but I'm more excited about BF4's Golmud Railway making its way to BF6

As promised, Battlefield Labs is coming back to bring us a preview of some of Battlefield 6’s upcoming Season 2 content.

Battlefield 6’s Season 2 was recently pushed back by a month to give Battlefield Studios time to polish up its content. Now, the developer has revealed how it plans to use some of that time, and the first port of call is Battlefield Labs.

As discussed in the initial delay message, BF Studios wants the community’s involvement earlier and more consistently in the development of future content. This includes Season 2, of course, and a big component of what it’s bringing to the game is headed to Labs.

The first Battlefield Labs session kicking off soon will focus on Contaminated, one of the new maps coming to Battlefield 6 with Season 2. BF Studios says the map falls between Eastwood and Mirak Valley, in terms of size.

The blog post even likened it to Battlefield 1’s St. Quentin Scar, and Battlefield 5’s Arras. Although we’ve yet to actually play it, the size and description do sound really well, especially in a game as starved of big maps as Battlefield 6 currently is.

Another thing BF Studios wants to test is the way ground vehicle gameplay and aerial presence interact with infantry combat, which is pretty standard for most Battlefield maps. Interestingly, there appears to be some sort of mechanic unique to Contaminated that the developer also wants to evaluate.

More Labs sessions are planned, including one that will show off new gameplay tools and vehicles. The AH-6 Little Bird helicopter was specifically namedropped, which makes sense given that it’s going to be part of Season 2’s content.

Battlefield Labs sessions will also extend beyond the biggest-ticket items of maps and vehicles. BF Studios said we should expect tests of upcoming features, like the Aircraft Radar, as part of a list of other air combat updates.

Ground vehicles, and they way the various rockets interact with them, will also be evaluated in a different session, with specific adjustments planned for RPGs and TOWs. And, of course, the work to improve and perfect hit reg remains ongoing, and future tweaks will go through Labs first.

There’s even more exciting news for fans of big maps, as the blog post also confirmed that Battlefield 4’s Golmud Railway is currently in the works, planned to go live in a future season. Golmud Railway will show up early in Labs, and you can expect it to evolve over multiple sessions.

For context, when it does arrive in Battlefield 6, Golmud Railway will be the largest map in the game, which is saying something. Though the map is beloved by vehicle players, it has its issues elsewhere, and BF Studios says it will be looking at all that when it creates the BF6, emphasising that it won’t be a simple port of the BF4 original.

Finally, the post throws a bone to Redsec battle royale players still waiting for a Solo mode. BF Studios continues to test the idea internally, but it’s taking a while. Needless to say, there are so many aspects that need to be considered. Game pace, balance, player survivability, match flow just to name a few.

Redsec BR was built with squads in mind, so that task is extra challenging. Though the developer didn’t say when we can expect Solos to arrive in Labs, players will get a chance to experience it before it enters the live game.

#4123. Vampire Therapist review - “The problems of unlife aren't so black and white.”

For over a century now, the vampire has fascinated humanity. From books to films, television and yes, even video games, the enigma of an undead bloodsucker that nonetheless has the wisdom of the ages is a contradiction we all seek to understand. Vampire Therapist isn’t concerned with tragic backstories or merciless sadism but with how to move past them.

In Vampire Therapist, you play undead cowboy Samuel Walls, who is invited to Germany by the three-thousand-year-old Andromachos. For some devious scheme? No, but to help other people. Vampires, that is. Because, as Samuel Walls, you are the one and only Vampire Therapist. And God help you, because these bloodsuckers have some problems.

How can I help you tonight? Vampire Therapist is a visual novel with puzzle elements where, as Walls, your job is to - surprise, surprise - provide psychological aid to your undead kin. To do so, you listen to their problems and aim to catch them in mental contradictions which hold them back from improving or seeing reality.

It can seem a little gamified, but there is definitely a fascinating deductive element to catching your client doing things like Labeling or Disqualifying the Positive, all of which seem to be real therapy terms, but which are explained in a digestible format. The focus is not on catching out your clients, but on taking advantage of these contradictions to show them where they can manage their problems.

You’ll also get to make occasional decisions on what to say or do, which can shift the story in different directions. The focus is mainly on the psychological element, and that in itself is enough to carry the whole game. In fact, I was a little miffed when it got interrupted by a blood-drinking minigame, not least because it was a little janky in the build which I played.

Whenever you have an issue, you can look back at your notes to study them for references to your client’s case files, as well as Sam’s notes that point to the issues they have. You can also look up definitions of the psychological contradictions, including some handy examples. Admittedly, I missed these on my playthrough, but they are there if you’re the journal-reading type, and Andromachos will be on hand to guide you through initial sessions anyway. The Looks and Sound of Death In visual terms, Vampire Therapist is your typical visual novel. You have character sprites with occasional shifts in pose and expression, while vivid backgrounds show which scene you’re in. The art style is a decent middle ground between realistic and stylised, meaning even the more stereotypical vampires, such as the half-century-old Renaissance aristocrat, aren’t boiled down to simple caricatures.

The music in Vampire Therapist is pretty simple, consisting of the main theme and occasional background noises. I did find the track that plays in the vampire club, which your patron Andromachos uses as his base of operations, a little repetitive, which can be an issue since you revisit it pretty frequently.

The voice acting, however, is undoubtedly a standout. Naturally, Matthew Mercer provides his vocal talent as incidental character Reinhard, and also appears later on in the full game. But Cyrus Nemati is a standout as Sam Walls, who provides cosy mix of stereotypical gravely cowboy and surprisingly self-aware, world-wise wanderer. What’s the story, morning glory? The actual narrative of Vampire Therapist is pretty engaging, and what we find out about Sam Walls, Andromachos and your clients such as Doctor Drayne (yes, really) and Isabella d’Este paints a fascinating picture of vampiric history. There are definitely shades of Underworld and Vampire: The Masquerade, but Vampire Therapist stays on the lighter side of things.

The motivations and backstory for your clients also manage to quite elegantly marry typical vampiric tropes with more realistic psychological conditions. Doctor Drayne struggles with addiction, only it’s to an experimental plasma he’s been making at his pharmaceutical company as part of a synthetic blood substitute.

The Contessa d’Este, meanwhile, is a literal Renaissance woman who struggles with depression and anger at the world, because after funding the great arts in her heyday, seeing Space Wars: Rise of Spacewalker (no prize for what that’s parodying) made her think all her efforts to enlighten humanity were for nought.

About the only issue I had is that Vampire Therapist, for what I played at least, seems to sidestep some more pressing issues and leaves a lot of questions unanswered about character motivations. Drayne, for example, is mostly concerned that his addiction to the experimental plasma is affecting his workaholic lifestyle, but the fact he has no memory of what happens when he consumes the substance isn’t given any attention at all.

Admittedly, it’d be a bit awkward to delve into Andromachos’ backstory as the Terror of the Mediterranean, and it might well be something brought up in latter parts of the story. Still, it can feel as though there are some elements that should be explored further, especially as we do get a lot of detail about Sam Walls’ path to redemption even in the first part of Vampire Therapist. What’s been biting at you this evening? Vampire Therapist doesn’t have much in the way of issues, as I see it. It’s a solid visual novel with an original premise, some intriguing puzzle gameplay and a genuinely fascinating, intriguing approach to explaining concepts of mental health and therapy that I found quite informative.

The only problem is that it does presume a lot about the player and how they want Sam Walls to act. Especially considering one early section has Walls nibbling (consensually) on some goth necks in a very sensually implied manner. It’s not as though you’re not warned that it delves into mature topics, but if you’re like me and couldn’t stand the romance in something like Baldur’s Gate 3 it can still feel a bit awkward.

But those are small potatoes, and my earlier mention of stuff I think the story could have done better is only evidence of how much I was paying attention to, and absorbing, the world and its characters, which I think is the highest praise you can give anything narrative-based. It’s lightweight, narrow in scale and perfect for relaxing while offering something of a challenge as you learn more about your clients and try to help them ground themselves and, if not resolve, then at least manage their problems. Let’s put a stake in this What I really liked about Vampire Therapist was how it connected the issues faced by immortals to real-world mental problems without seeming hokey. It’s not just that the Contessa is feeling depressed; it’s that seeing the world go from the Mona Lisa to Rise of Skywalker has seemingly given her concrete evidence that her years of patronage to the fine arts were worthless.

This makes Vampire Therapist feel worthwhile for fans of vampire fiction, as well as those just looking for a fascinating story. Add to that the intriguing explanations of therapy terms, psychological distortions and explorations of the (in)human condition, and ironically it feels as though a game about vampires helps to demystify the idea.

If you’re looking for a solid visual novel with a bit of meat on its bones, and some great art and audio that elevates what rather bashfully calls itself a low-budget indie, then Vampire Therapist is a must-play!

We’re expecting a content update each month, with the majority of the biggest additions happening on the game’s existing maps. There is, however, at least one new map in the works, but it won’t be here until sometime in April.

While we wait for that, Arc Raiders is going to go through several events and other in-game changes, some more meaningful (and exciting) than others. January looks to be the lightest so far, which makes sense given that it’s just a week or so from ending.

Things start getting interesting in February, when Shrouded Sky will begin. This chapter brings three exciting additions to Arc Raiders. There will be a new Map Condition, new Arc Threat, and the start of another Player Project.

#4117. Marvel 1943: Rise Of Hydra Reportedly Still In Development Amid Rumors Of Its Cancellation

Yesterday, a rumor emerged on X claiming that Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra, the upcoming World War II-era superhero game led by Uncharted creator Amy Hennig, was being cancelled. After making the rounds on social media, new reports claim this is not the case, at least for now.

The rumor stemmed from a now-deleted X post from a fan account called Marvel 1943 Rise Of Hydra Countdown claiming, through supposed inside sources, that Skydance was preparing to announce the game’s cancellation. This rumor was quickly picked up and circulated by online gaming circles, gaining steam due to growing uncertainty around the game’s status.

Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra was revealed in 2022 and stars Captain America and Black Panther (Azurri, T'Challa's grandfather), alongside Howling Commandos member Gabriel Jones and Wakandan Spy Network leader Nanali, as they battle Hydra during World War II. Developed by Skydance New Media, led by Amy Hennig, it’s been repeatedly delayed, and only cinematic footage has been released. This has understandably caused many to question the game’s fate.

However, a few hours after the cancellation rumor made the rounds, Bloomberg’s Jason Schreier reported on Bluesky that Skydance’s leadership addressed the rumor with the development team on Slack and assured them Marvel 1943 was not canceled. However, Schreier adds this could change due to the uncertainty caused by the recent merger between Warner Bros. Discovery and Paramount Skydance (Skydance New Media is a game development branch of the now-merged Skydance Corporation).

Skydance Games told the development team behind Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra on Slack this afternoon that the game is not canceled, despite a widely circulated rumor on Twitter today claiming that it was.

Furthermore, Kotaku’s Rebekah Valentine clarified in her report that Marvel 1943 executive producer Lu Giglotti told staff in a Skydance Slack message he’d spoken directly with the executive leadership team to confirm Marvel 1943 is still alive, saying, "There is no truth to these claims." According to Kotaku’s report, Giglotti informed the team that Marvel 1943 was approaching an Alpha milestone later this month. Giglotti also told staff not to let the rumor distract them and that Skydance was "monitoring the situation" to address in the future.

Kotaku’s report also sheds light on the game’s tumultuous development cycle. Marvel 1943 was originally pitched as a Netflix game before it was eventually turned into a console and PC title. This transition means the current iteration is “light on gameplay” and lacks substantial interactions, with players primarily using a single button to play it.

This isn't a completely surprising revelation, as Marvel 1943 was billed as a narrative-driven, linear single-player experience when it was revealed, but the style of game has never been clear. The same reveal also saw Skydance promise the game boasted "intuitive controls and exhilarating second-to-second gameplay that captures the action and excitement of Marvel, inspired by landmark comics, television, and films, as they navigate this all-new globe-trotting adventure." This disconnect may be attributed to Kotaku also reporting that Marvel 1943 is “well over budget,” and its overall scope has been heavily scaled back. Regardless, the outlet’s source claims the game is “close to done.”

Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra was initially slated to launch in 2025. It was then delayed to early 2026 "to add more polish", according to Skydance, before being pushed again to an undetermined launch window. The game has no announced platforms.

Although Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra appears safe for now, other recent projects have not been as fortunate. Be sure to read our stories about the recent high-profile cancellations of Gang of Dragon and Fairgames.

#4116. GTA 6: Near Fatal Sex Scandal Guide

Michael Manning (He/Him) has been enamored with video games since he first played the Sonic Classic Collection as a child. With decades of experience in gaming and a full tour as a Gaming Journalist, Michael is ready to step up to the plate. From AAA to the smallest passion projects, his motto is that every piece of ar

Grand Theft Auto has never shied away from, well, anything really. Political corruption, gang violence, culture clashes, both the underworld and sleazy heights are well within Rockstar’s sights, both in their main campaigns and plethora of side content.

Even with the many easter eggs in GTA 6, you wouldn't expect time travel to be one of them. But you can do it if you're persistent enough to follow a meticulously planned order of steps.

With Grand Theft Auto 6’s small-scale start, it can be easy to forget that, with various side missions here to remind us. One such mission without a name, one I’ll just be calling the Near Fatal Sex Scandal, sees a woman begging for help on the side of the road. Want to learn more, and even how to start it yourself? Let’s get straight to it then.

While driving down the US-70 post Chapter 2, you may hear a woman crying for help, clad in a bathrobe. If you stop to help her, she’ll explain that someone up by the house needs your help, and beg you to follow.

Follow her, and she’ll escort you through a very fancy southern style manor, before approaching a bedroom. She asks for your complete confidentiality before opening the door, revealing her husband, a right-wing politician, unresponsive in a sex swing.

Interact with the body to help her get him down, where she’ll realize he’s already dead. Quick on her feet, she demands you help dispose of the body, pointing you to the river just down the hill as the perfect spot. Pick up the corpse as she rushes you out to continue.

As you carry the body down the hill, the politician himself will begin to stir, startling the player character, who drops him to the grass. Stunned and betrayed by his wife’s seeming attempt on his life, he’ll demand you back him up. Follow him back to the estate and allow him to interact with the bedroom door.

His wife, again not missing a beat, immediately pivots back into their roleplay, belittling him and yanking her “bad little globalist” back into the bedroom. For your trouble (and trauma), you’re tossed a cool $10,000, an absolute game changer if found early enough in Chapter 2.

Grand Theft Auto 6 is back to its seams with all kinds of small encounters like this, perfect for a quick joke and a pocket full of cash as you pursue Jason and Lucia’s perfect life.

GodLike Esports beat Trigger Point Esports 2-0 in the upper bracket of the VCT Pacific Kickoff South Asia qualifier. Only two South Asian sides will reach the Last Chance Qualifier, where a single place at Kickoff in Bangkok is on offer.

GodLike Esports opened their VCT Pacific Kickoff: South Asia – Qualifier 2027 playoff campaign with a 2-0 win over Trigger Point Esports on Monday 23 November 2026. GodLike took both maps of the best-of-three upper bracket quarter-final. Trigger Point Esports now drop into the lower bracket of the double-elimination format.

The playoffs are being held online by Riot Games and JioBLAST. Series in the bracket are played as best-of-three or best-of-five.

GodLike arrived in form. They reached the playoffs with an unbeaten 4-0 record in the open qualifier, VLR.gg reported. They shared joint first to fourth place in that event, which ran from 17 to 20 November. Trigger Point finished in the group placed fifth to eighth.

GodLike fielded Karam1L, Paradox and RvK from India, alongside sayoo from Indonesia and azyshaha from the Philippines. Sabyasachi ‘Antidote’ Bose is listed as head coach, with Samar as substitute. Trigger Point’s listed players are SangraM, WEELJACK and RaJ.

South Asian teams cannot qualify directly for Kickoff. The top two from the playoffs join the Oceania playoff winner and the Southeast Asia playoff runner-up in a four-team Last Chance Qualifier. Only its winner goes through to Kickoff in Bangkok, according to Dot Esports.

The stakes are high. Twelve teams will play at Kickoff, and the top three will qualify for Masters 1. The route stays narrow later in the season too. South Asia has no direct place at the Cups, with Cup 1 in Manila and Cup 2 in Tokyo. It sends two teams to an eight-team Pacific LCQ, and the winner takes the last Cup place.

The qualifier also has a new organiser. Riot picked JioBLAST to run the South Asia qualifiers instead of NODWIN Gaming, the previous organiser. Riot has not said why it made the change.

The UK interest lies with SIGN Esports. They beat Zexar Esports 2-0 in another upper bracket quarter-final. Russel ‘Russ’ Mendes joined SIGN Esports on 16 November 2026. He is the only player from the UK in the eight-team playoff field.

Russ was born in 1998 and is of Indian descent. He won the VALORANT Challengers 2025 South Asia Grand Final with Velocity Gaming on 13 July 2025, when they beat S8UL 3-1.

GodLike Esports and SIGN Esports both remain in the upper bracket, one defeat away from the lower bracket. Trigger Point Esports and Zexar Esports must win from the lower bracket to stay in contention for a top-two finish. The playoffs run until 29 November 2026.

Nioh 3 is one of the most anticipated games of 2026, and it’s easily among the biggest releases of February. We’re a few days away from the start of that month, however, but we don’t have to wait until then to actually play Team Ninja’s next major release.

#4112. 10 Fighting Game Remakes That Improved Everything From The Original Games

Manuel Sifontes is a content strategist and multimedia journalist specializing in technology, culture, and storytelling. He crafts clear, engaging narratives and builds digital audience growth.

I still look back fondly on those afternoons at my grandmother's house, sitting in front of the TV with my cousins and firing up my PlayStation 1 for hours of fighting games like Tekken 3—a series I'm still playing with Tekken 8—and Mortal Kombat Trilogy, one of the best games with non-stop violence that ever existed.

Still, the genre hasn't always been perfect. Plenty of classics launched with serious balance issues, rough performance, or questionable mechanics that could easily sour the experience.

Fortunately, some of those games got a second chance through exceptional remakes that fixed every flaw from the originals. Here are 10 fighting games that completely reinvented themselves with new mechanics, features and definitive balancing.

As a longtime JoJo's Bizarre Adventure fan, I was excited when All-Star Battle got its Western PS3 release in 2014 (following its 2013 Japanese debut). That hype faded fast once I felt its 30 fps frame rate, slower combat pacing, and a Campaign mode weighed down by stamina timers and microtransactions.

In 2022, Bandai Namco released JoJo's Bizarre Adventure: All-Star Battle R on PS4, PS5, Xbox One, Xbox Series X/S, Switch, and PC. While the Switch version runs at 30 fps, the PlayStation, Xbox, and PC editions target 60 fps, immediately making combat feel snappier to me. It also added an Assist system for extending combos and expanded the roster across the series.

Best of all, it dropped the original Campaign's stamina timers and energy purchases—though the game still features paid DLC characters and costumes, and solo players lost the original Story and Campaign modes in favor of the panel-based All-Star Battle mode. For me, the faster gameplay made that trade-off worth it.

Not every necessary remake is modern. While the 1993 arcade Virtua Fighter was a landmark title, its 1994 Sega Saturn port was rough, with flat, untextured polygonal models and distracting polygon flickering.

Released in 1995 for arcades and the Saturn, Virtua Fighter Remix tackled those early-port issues head-on. Side by side on Saturn, the jump is clear: Remix introduced texture-mapped character models with far sharper facial and outfit detail. It wasn't a flawless fix—some polygon glitches remained, the lighting shifted, and load times increased—but for Saturn owners at the time, it was still a major visual upgrade that stood up much better alongside early Tekken.

Video game studios have done a great job of bringing retro fighting games to modern platforms, but a few are still trapped on antiquated systems.

After falling in love with Bloody Roar 2, playing Bloody Roar 3 on PS2 (following its 2000 arcade debut) left me wanting more. Its animal-transformation premise was still a blast, but to my eyes, the early-PS2 visuals looked rough, with jagged edges and coarse textures.

In 2002, Bloody Roar: Primal Fury launched on Nintendo GameCube (followed by Bloody Roar Extreme on Xbox in 2003) as an enhanced remake of Bloody Roar 3. Compared to the PS2 release, the GameCube version offered cleaner character models, upgraded lighting, animated endings for the cast, and newcomers like Cronos and Ganesha. Personally, it became my go-to way to play the game, making every match feel far more polished and satisfying.

I've loved Street Fighter for years, but jumping into specific Western arcade revisions of 1994's Super Street Fighter II Turbo—notably the World 940223 and USA 940323 builds—was a rude awakening. Both are notorious for a difficulty bug that makes the CPU unusually fierce regardless of the machine's setting, on top of lopsided matchups involving Old Sagat, Vega, and a tournament-banned Akuma.

When Super Street Fighter II Turbo HD Remix hit PS3 and Xbox 360 in 2008, I was immediately won over. Udon Entertainment redrew the sprites and stages in HD, and the game added a rebalanced mode to rein in dominant fighters while still letting purists play under the original rules. Paired with built-in GGPO rollback netcode, it became a much friendlier way to enjoy a classic.

The PS2 introduced me to countless classics, including Dead or Alive 2: Hardcore (an updated PS2 edition of the 1999 arcade and 2000 Dreamcast fighter). I loved its fast pace and multi-tiered stages, though its early-PS2 visuals aged quickly and its counter-heavy combat could feel unforgiving.

Dead or Alive Ultimate arrived on the original Xbox in 2004 with a ground-up remake of DOA2 built on an upgraded DOA3 engine. Compared to the PS2 version, the leap in lighting, textures, and stage detail was night and day. While reversals remained a defining—and sometimes divisive—part of the formula, Ultimate felt like the definitive package, bringing together fighters like Tengu and Bayman alongside DOA3's Hitomi and over 20 interactive stages.

At launch, it also stood out for its Xbox Live lobbies and spectator mode—a huge draw at the time, even though Microsoft officially shut down original Xbox Live servers in April 2010.

The PlayStation 2 brought some incredible fighting games during its lifetime. This list breaks down the 10 best to grace the PS2 system.

SNK's catalog deserves a spot in any fighting game discussion, including The King of Fighters 2002. This fantastic Neo Geo game had strong core gameplay, but its presentation felt more stripped-back to me than SNK's earlier classics, with a soundtrack that didn't hit as hard and several NESTS-saga favorites missing from the roster.

I also wasn't a fan of a meta dominated by Billy Kane, Athena, and Choi. That's why the 2009 remake, The King of Fighters 2002: Unlimited Match (originally on PS2, later coming to Xbox Live Arcade in 2010 and PC in 2015), felt like such a triumph.

Expanding the roster to 66 playable characters in its console and Xbox Live Arcade editions, it overhauled the stages (using 3D polygonal backgrounds on PS2 and 2D replacements on PC), added a new soundtrack, refined MAX Mode cancels, and introduced new moves across the cast—turning it into one of my favorite 2D fighters SNK has ever made.

The original Karateka launched in 1984 for the Apple II before receiving ports for Atari 8-bit systems, the NES/Famicom, and the Commodore 64. Its flaws stood out quickly, though: the controls were slow and stiff, there were no checkpoints—meaning a single lost fight sent you right back to the beginning—and the combat system was bare-bones.

In 2012, however, a remake arrived on Xbox 360 before making its way to PC, PS3, and iOS. This new version rebuilt the visuals from the ground up in cel-shaded 3D powered by Unreal Engine 3, and introduced a one-on-one combat system built around visual and audio cues for countering attacks. What really won me over was how it replaced the single-life structure with three consecutive suitors, each with different speeds and their own unique endings.

At launch, the original Fatal Fury: King of Fighters—released in 1991 for Neo Geo—drew plenty of criticism for offering only three playable characters: Andy Bogard, Terry Bogard, and Joe Higashi. On top of that, its gameplay lacked depth, relying on a simple three-button control scheme.

In 1999, Fatal Fury: Wild Ambition hit the Hyper Neo Geo 64 and PlayStation 1, expanding the roster to 12 fighters in arcades and 14 on PS1. It also introduced new defensive and meter-management mechanics, including the Heat Meter, Heat Blow, and Overdrive Power. It's worth noting, however, that Sony's console version took several noticeable graphical downgrades compared to the arcade release.

If you're a fan of weird and wonderful brawlers, here are several more obscure fighting games that are worth experiencing.

This title might not be as widely known as others on this list, but it had a strong following in Japan back in the day. Asuka 120% Burning Fest. originally launched in 1994 for the FM Towns, though several issues held the experience back—including a limited roster, a lack of defensive tools, and the fact that it was locked to a niche Japanese home computer.

Several years later, in 1999, Asuka 120% Final: Burning Fest. Final arrived on PS1. While it remained a Japan-only release, this version featured a completely rebuilt combat engine with a much faster pace and noticeably smoother sprite animations. It also expanded the character roster—adding secret fighters into the mix—and introduced deeper offensive and defensive mechanics, such as air recovery.

The original Eternal Champions launched on the Sega Genesis/Mega Drive in 1993 in North America, followed by Europe and Japan in 1994. Like many entries on this list, though, it suffered from frustrating issues—including punishing AI, clunky, unintuitive controls, and a small roster, among other flaws.

It wasn't until 1995 that its remake, Eternal Champions: Challenge from the Dark Side, which can be considered one of the best fighting games stuck on older systems, arrived on the Sega CD as an expanded overhaul of the original. It expanded the starting roster from nine to 13 fighters—alongside a large lineup of unlockables—introduced new FMV finishers called Cinekills, and improved the difficulty curve compared to the original game.

#4109. Infinity Nikki ushers in the Year of the Horse with... a deer-themed Version 2.2

Chromatic Beings Everbright, the latest major Infinity Nikki update, has arrived, bringing Chinese New Year celebrations vibe to the game.

Infinity Nikki, the free-to-play, open-world dress-up RPG, has delivered yet another big content drop in the form of Chromatic Beings Everbright. The latest update brings the game up to version 2.2, and introduces a new narrative chapter, and gameplay taking place around a festival narrative.

If you couldn’t guess already, the new theme is Bloom Festival, inspired by Chinese New Year celebrations.

The big new story chapter takes place in the Infinity Nikki’s Wanxiang Realm. This deceptively serene and blissful region hides a dark secret, however. Chromafaces, the mythical inhabitants of the realm, have to embody fixed identities that dictate how they live and work.

These are doled out through Character Tokens, which are used to assign roles to each individual. The story follows Nikki as she uncovers the script that runs the realm and the facade it props up. Nikki will help free Chromafaces and dispel the illusion.

The Wanxiang Realm is split into three areas. Cai Ye is your typical lantern-lit district, where festivals and fireworks happen. Kongming Gorge is almost the opposite of that; a quiet and cold place. Finally, Jiuhua Pavilion literally floats above the region, and it's home to neverending music and dance.

The other big addition in 2.2 are the two new 5-Star Resonance Outfits with some interesting gameplay implications. Where Wanxiang Weaves Life is inspired by wuxia aesthetics, and true to its inspirations, it lets Nikki shapeshift into different Spirit Personas - and automatically collect resources in her vicinity.

Chroma's Mortal Heart, on the other hand, allows Nikki to fly around the Wanxiang Realm, drawing on the power of the Celestial Deer. This outfit also uses Celestial Deer Vision to automatically ping and mark treasure chests around her.

You can also look forward to Nefarious Shadows, a new Ability Outfit, which lets Nikki see through disguises, and reveals hidden paths in the world.

As with every major update, of course, there are themed activities and limited-time events throughout. Hotpot House is a cooking minigame where you attempt to run the eponymous restaurant, whereas Flavor Frenzy is series of platforming challenges that tasks you with gathering ingredients. Fortune Mahjong is a little more straightforward, with support for solo and multiplayer play.

If you’re jumping back into the game soon, be sure to hit up our Infinity Nikki codes page for some freebies.

#4108. 10 Best Early Game Weapons in GTA VI

Shane is a Contributor for DualShockers writing guides and other materials. He has a degree in Game Design and Criticism.

In Vice City, you can never come too prepared for a fight. Between the nightlife and our protagonist's penchant for causing chaos, it’s a good idea to stay strapped in case of an emergency.

The only issue is that in those opening hours, you’re pretty limited in what you can get because money is fairly tight. If you’re looking to buy guns, you don’t want to waste your money on something that feels suboptimal.

ATM machines hold a lot of cash in GTA 6. Learn how to break them open and steal everything inside with this guide.

This list includes a bunch of good weapons you can get in the first couple of chapters of the game. It feels a little crazy that the early game can stretch so far in hours, but GTA 6 really is a humongous game.

The Duval Signature ES9 is basically a more powerful version of Jason’s starting weapon, and it’s a great weapon to keep on you at all times. While it is a sidearm, it can still be helpful in all kinds of situations.

The key part of this one is that it has incredibly high handling, meaning you’ll pretty much always hit what you aim for. In the early hours of the game, that can be the difference between life and death.

At a certain point in the game, you’ll be able to grab Donnie’s sidearm and keep it for yourself. This small but mighty weapon is great for people looking to take people out quickly at a shorter range.

You won’t be able to take on a whole army with it, but it fits nicely into an extra slot for when things start to get a little dicey. Donnie is a crazy guy, so it makes sense his gun is just a little crazy too.

Most people will probably feel like a sniper is relatively useless, especially when the cops start to roll up on you. For the most part, that’s true, but with this weapon you can easily take out some people without getting spotted.

With high range, accuracy, and decent damage, you can put down just about anything you come across with relative ease. Just be sure you’re far enough away to not have to worry about when people start looking.

This weapon is an alternative assault rifle you can buy called a battle rifle, and it comes in handy when going up against big crowds of enemies. Not only does it pack a good punch, but you can stay in relative safety while using it.

The only real downside to this one is that using it a little too much might see you moving in a negative way with your Criminal Profile. That’s probably something you’re going to want to avoid if you’re hoping to stick to a happy ending.

This lovely little piece does a great job at putting just about anything down, but you’ll still need to be choosy about how you fire. It does have great handling, but you could still find yourself in real danger if you get surrounded quickly.

Aside from that, it’s a great weapon for car fights since it can pack such a good punch. If you’ve got the aim to use it, this bad boy can take on most any challenge, except maybe some truly unhinged NPCs.

If you are having trouble finding yourself a plane in GTA VI, this guide is for you.

A fancy found weapon, the Scrapper VF5C, is a great weapon to get, especially before you start getting into the really crazy parts of the game. Silenced and ready for action, this gun will be a great tool for taking on even the toughest jobs.

It does lack some stopping power, but with such high handling, it’s relatively easy to use, and that’s a very good thing. As long as you’re smart with it, there’s virtually nothing this weapon can’t handle.

One of the best early-game weapons that you can grab basically right at the start is the Wortham W-14. It’s a little tough to use, but once you have the hang of it, you can put down anyone who crosses your path.

It’s a fantastic weapon, especially if you’re looking to keep your Criminal Profile on the lighter side. One shot is really all you need with this one, and with such high accuracy, it hardly ever misses the mark.

Probably the best early-game longarm weapon you can get, this found weapon will make swiss cheese out of anyone you want. It’s got high damage and good handling, but you’ll be on your own for aiming and distance.

This gun is phenomenal for almost any scenario, but especially in situations where you’re running into a lot of people. Whether it’s the foot or the face, you’ll only ever need to shoot once at someone to take them out of the fight.

Of course, it wouldn’t be a Rockstar game without including some choice references, and what a reference it is. With this lovely piece as a nod to Red Dead Redemption, you’ll find yourself operating like a real cowboy on the streets of Vice City.

The gun is only available as part of the Ultimate Edition, which is a little problematic, but despite that, it isn’t the only powerful early-game sidearm. It does pack quite the punch and lets you pick off enemies from a distance.

The best early-game weapon of all is a found weapon you can get from pretty much the opening hours of the game. This small silenced pistol is great for committing all kinds of nefarious acts without ever having to worry about getting caught.

While its damage is low, it’ll never give away your position and can quickly put holes in people with ease. It works best if you’re looking to avoid complete shootouts, but really you could pretty much use it whenever in this insanely good simulation game.

#4107. God Of War Sons Of Sparta Gets PS4 Version And New Content Next Monday

It's been about nine months since Sony Santa Monica and Mega Cat Studios dropped God of War Sons of Sparta as a surprise reveal and launch during a State of Play. If you haven't checked it out yet, the developers are giving you some new reasons to today, unveiling two new modes and a new platform: PlayStation 4.

If you don't remember, God of War Sons of Sparta is a prequel spin-off of the God of War series, showing protagonist Kratos as a 13-year-old soldier, long before his god-killing days. The game features 2D combat and a Metroidvania-style map, along with a fully voiced cast of characters including Scott Menville (who you might recognize as Robin in Teen Titans) as Kratos' brother Deimos, Jack Quaid (who will voice a different character in God of War Laufey next year), and TC Carson, who returns from the original trilogy as the voice of adult Kratos.

Announced in a post on the PlayStation Blog today, Sons of Sparta is making the jump back to Sony's previous console, which is now (brace yourself) 13 years old. Sons of Sparta's 2D pixel art is far less demanding than the other God of War entries, though, so it's no surprise this was possible – it's mainly surprising that they're doing it at all.

For PS5 players who already own the game, developer Mega Cat is also adding two new modes: Hermes Mode and Erebus Mode. Hermes Mode, named after the Greek god of wind, mail, and speed, is a speedrun mode that encourages you to beat the game as quickly as possible, complete with a split-based timer in the upper right-hand corner of the screen. Meanwhile, Erebus Mode, named after one of the domains of the underworld (you'll be familiar with it if you've played the Hades games), makes the game far deadlier as Kratos and all his foes die in a single hit. You'll have to wait until you beat the game once to unlock Erebus Mode, but you can access Hermes Mode from a fresh save by entering the following (and semi-familiar) code in the start menu: Up, Up, Down, Down, Left, Right, Left, Right, L1, R1, Touchpad.

The free update and PS4 version will be available next Monday, November 16, at midnight local time. For more Sons of Sparta, check out our review. For more God of War, bad news: God of War Laufey was just delayed until May.

#4106. Feature: Don't Have Your Wii Set Up? Here Are 20 Wii Games You Can Play On Switch

Many people reading this will have a Wii in the house. Even if it's collecting dust in the cupboard after launching 20 years ago, there's over 100 million of the things out in the wild, so the chances are that you or your family have access to one somewhere.

However, on the off-chance you don't have a Wii to hand — or you sold it years ago to save three DVDs' worth of space — don't fret. While the system has a selection of exclusives you can't easily play elsewhere, many Wii games have come to Switch in HD remastered form over the years.

So if you're jonesing for some Wii waggle but would rather use the Nintendo console already plugged into the telly, take a look at some of the highlights below, in alphabetical order.

A Switch remaster of WayForward's remake of the NES original, A Boy and His Blob hasn’t changed since its release back in 2009, but it’s well worth checking out if you’re after a decent puzzle platformer. The visuals still look incredible after all these years, with spectacular animation to boot.

Some aspects feel a bit outdated by comparison to more modern alternatives, with the inability to map certain abilities being a key culprit. Nevertheless, it remains a fun, breezy experience, and one that the younger generation of gamers in particular will adore.

This Nintendo-published remake includes not just DS' Another Code: Two Memories, or Trace Memory in North America, but also the Wii sequel Another Code R, A Journey Into Lost Memories (which never came out in North America).

This is a fine reworking of a couple of point-and-click cult classics from now-defunct studio Cing (who also did the excellent Little King's Story), with a touching narrative, weighty themes, and light puzzling.

Please note that some external links on this page are affiliate links, which means if you click them and make a purchase we may receive a small percentage of the sale. Please read our FTC Disclosure for more information.

Available separately or bundled in the BIT.TRIP COLLECTION, this was the first entry in Commander Video's Runner series, and both Runner 2 and 3 are on Switch eShop if you want the trilogy.

The WiiWare original garnered a 10/10 on this very website back in 2010. Worth a look, then.

In the great platformer pantheon, we're not talking all-timers here, but these are slick, solid efforts with plenty of personality. Both de Blob and its sequel are on Switch in HD form, so if you're jonesing to see how devs approached 3D platformers in the late 2000s, get this inked in your diary.

Epic Mickey was a bold and very fine piece of work, although one where you could still make out the work-in-progress ideas that didn't quite come to fruition with the level of polish Nintendo fans might expect. It reimagined the squeaky-clean mascot and put him in a much darker world than we had come to expect, adding a touching narrative and putting a spotlight on his 'forgotten' predecessor, Oswald the Rabbit.

The Rebrushed remaster makes some tweaks and adds mouse (heh) controls. One for fans of vintage animation and anyone who likes to see creators take exciting chances with the most established of properties.

Soapbox 10 Years On, We Need More Brave, Worthwhile Experiments Like Epic Mickey

Donkey Kong Country Returns HD is a fine way to play the 2010 original, but it’s also lacking any real reason for fans to double-dip beyond waggle-free controls. It’s less of a remaster and more of a port, which would be all well and good if it wasn’t being sold at such a premium. Maybe wait for a sale.

There's plenty of fun to be had, but grab the superior Donkey Kong Country: Tropical Freeze instead - or at least first.

A 2023 Deluxe remaster of 2010's original Return to Dream Land, the HD Switch version threw in various tweaks, a couple of new copy abilities, an epilogue with Magalor, and an assortment of minigames mostly cherry-picked from past Kirby games.

Worth a look even if you've played the original to death, and the choice pick if you never had the pleasure.

Klonoa started out on PlayStation, of course, with Door to Phantomile back in 1997. Lunatea's Veil followed on PS2 in 2001, and Klonoa Phantasy Reverie Series bundles remasters of them both into a single Switch package.

So why this here at all!? yells the person at the back who's been grumbling ever since they saw the lead image on the article.

Well, although developer Monkey Craft tweaked some elements to push it closer to Namco's PS1 original in look and feel, the first remaster here uses Paon's Wii remake as its foundation. So if you played the Wii version in 2008, you'll be right at home.

The 2011 WiiWare release was a remake of the PC original, but fortunately La-Mulana found its way to Switch in 2020 (alongside its sequel).

Though brilliant, La-Mulana is definitely one of those games that will only appeal to a dedicated few. This is not something you can casually play every once in a while and expect a great experience; it demands much more of you through its peerless puzzle design.

If you do give it the time of day, however, it proves itself to be one of the most intricately crafted Metroidvanias ever made. La-Mulana gets a strong recommendation, but with the caveat that you should expect to be frustrated and stuck often. Don’t be scared off by the daunting difficulty, though; this is one for the ages.

A sneaky early addition here, as this remaster of Vanillaware's Wii (and Vita) game isn't out until 4th February 2027.

A gorgeous side-on action RPG, 2009's Muramasa: The Demon Blade was ahead of the wave of side-scrolling platformers that would arrive from indie studios over the next few years, and its eye-catching adventure through Japanese folklore is still a treat many years later.

Definitely one to look out for in the new year.

Soapbox Vanillaware's Most Underrated Game Is More Than Just A Pretty Picture

Probably cult developer Suda51's most well-known work, No More Heroes came to Switch in 2020 along with its sequel ahead of No More Heroes III's launch the following year.

Crammed with okatu-fuelled pop culture references (but hailing from nearly 20 years when those references weren't quite so tired), this was an adrenaline shot for Wii owners in 2007 looking for something a bit different after a year of genial waggle.

Wii scored not one, but two Touchdowns (and Switch has so far doubled that). Grasshopper returned with a punchy sequel in 2010, which once again helped put some personality on the Wii shelves alongside all the sanitised, motion-based sports and party fare.

Ironing out some of the wrinkles of the original and throwing plenty more irreverence and off-the-wall antics from the mind of Goichi Suda, No More Heroes 2: Desperate Struggle is still the peak of the trilogy for many.

It may have debuted on the PS2, but Ready at Dawn's Wii port felt like a minor miracle back in 2008. It's a great game that came to Wii, and you can play it on Switch, so here it is!

Okami HD is an utterly fantastic piece of software; a 40-hour adventure that emulates Zelda wonderfully, adds in plenty of memorable mechanics, features one of the most beautiful art styles in gaming, and is completely playable on the go, to boot.

It may be showing its age a bit visually and its combat is sometimes a little on the easy side, but Okami is an important, fun, and notable landmark in gaming history — and one of the easiest recommendations for your Switch library.

Stretching things a little here, both Pikmin and Pikmin 2: This Time It's Pikminable* were both GameCube games that got Wii-specific releases in the New Play Control series which added pointer controls and other minor tweaks.

Both games are available on Switch, though, so I'm including them. In fact, all four mainline Pikmin games are playable on Switch, something which irritates Metroid Prime fans no end.

*I enjoy the idea that this could turn up in somebody's AI summary. Ah, it's the little pleasures that get us through the day.

Perhaps the best thing about Sonic Colors Ultimate is the menu option to change the logo and UI from the American English 'Colors' to the British English 'Colours', mirroring the regional variants of the original 2010 Wii release. Great attention to detail, and an example of the care and respect that went into this solid remaster.*

*Don't forget, you have to have a little fun every day.

Regardless of which you think is better, these are two of the finest platformers ever made, both on Switch and looking better than ever.

Nursing the gyro pointers is a minor irritation the originals didn't suffer from, but if you somehow missed either of these on the Wii, you've now got no excuse.

Buy Super Mario Galaxy + Super Mario Galaxy 2

Bringing the Wii launch game back with a lick of HD 13 years later, Banana Blitz HD featured more refined controls — or more specifically let you control the mazes with the analogue stick — to help you enjoy this batch of 100 levels.

The wider game was still let down by weird leaderboard decisions and some lacklustre minigames, though. Hardly a return to the monkey-in-a-ball heyday of Super Monkey Ball 2, but not bad.

The Legend of Zelda: Skyward Sword HD introduced a raft of technical improvements and quality-of-life updates that revitalised the Wii game.

The alternate button control scheme totally worked if you still couldn't get on with the motion controls, the graphics got a sensitively handled HD overhaul, and a once-bothersome sidekick was streamlined into something altogether more useful. The best way to play.

World of Goo is a bona fide indie classic and 10/10 video game in its original incarnation. Its Wii pointer controls married perfectly with the gooey puzzling, and the social satire provided a subtle narrative framework that elevated the entire game.

The Switch version comes with joys and cons. Touchscreen is a brilliant addition in handheld mode, but you'll need to recentre the gyro pointer controls a lot. A lot.

If you've played it previously, the Switch incarnation might be worth a second go for its portability and on-the-go co-op, but if it's your first time in the World of Goo, it's absolutely a must-play. And then there's the sequel to consider. There's goo in them there hills.

The third iteration of Monolith Soft's classic following the Wii original and the New 3DS version in 2015, Xenoblade Chronicles: Definitive Edition presented an already excellent JRPG improved in nearly every way, short of a complete reimagining.

With the Nintendo Switch 2 Edition polishing this gem even further, it's hard to recommend the original release these days unless you're a purist wanting the exact experience everyone else got back in 2011. This is a great update, and a worthy game to finish on.

Buy Xenoblade Chronicles: Definitive Edition – Nintendo Switch 2 Edition

A pleasant little selection, no? Before heading off, let's address a handful of questions...

Yes, I know there are technically 22+ here. The Pikmins were borderline and bundled, though, and there are two Mario Galaxies in a single entry, a couple of other fuzzy collections, and Muramasa isn't even out yet. It all comes out in the wash.

Not impossible! Presumably it would be Switch 2-only (as with the GameCube library). It would be simple enough for Nintendo to produce NSO Wii Remotes and Nunchuk controllers, as they have for previous retro consoles.

There are potential flies in the ointment, though. For one thing, the precision of the infrared Wii pointer would either need to be emulated with gyro or reproduced (meaning you'd need some sort of sensor bar equivalent to function with the new controllers). Either or both are possibilities, but it does introduce another layer of complexity.

Then again, we're talking about a company that requires an expensive Virtual Boy facsimile to access that system's library on Switch, so (much) stranger things have happened.

As for the library itself, as we've seen above, several first-party Wii games have already received the HD treatment on Switch, so there may be less incentive on Nintendo's side to duplicate those on NSO. Likewise, Switch Sports and Switch Sports Resort update many of the games from the Wii originals, so it's not like you can't play Wii Sports-style tennis already.

But bolstered with a good selection of third-party titles, a Wii NSO library could be a winner.

Along with our list of Wii exclusives (or, in a couple of cases, games originally released on Wii that only appeared elsewhere years later), I'd do bad things for a 4K remaster of the beautiful Kirby's Epic Yarn.

It would be great to have access to other exclusives like New Super Mario Bros. Wii - not everyone's favourite 2D Mario, but an important one. Likewise, it's a shame to have Super Paper Mario and other entries from big Nintendo series (hello, Radiant Dawn) locked to a 20-year-old platform.

But that's me - what about you? Let us know below which of the games above you've enjoyed most, and any others you've enjoyed revisiting on Switch.

#4105. Metal Gear Solid 4: Guns Of The Patriots: Part 8 – A Nostalgic Island Getaway | Super Replay

In 2008, Kojima Productions released what was billed as the swan song for Hideo Kojima's Metal Gear series: Metal Gear Solid 4: Guns of the Patriots. The game had the staggering task of tying up decades of storytelling by bringing together Solid Snake, Ocelot, Otacon, Raiden, and many more characters for one explosive finale. The adventure centers on a rapidly aging Solid Snake racing against the clock to stop his twin and nemesis, Liquid Snake, one last time. Of course, there are far more bizarre shenanigans at play.

Guns of the Patriots was acclaimed for its storytelling, cinematic presentation, and evolution of the series' stealth gameplay, namely the OctoCamo suit that allowed Snake to mimic the appearance/texture of any surface he touched. It also has the distinct honor of earning a rare 10/10 review score from Game Informer. Now, thanks to the Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2, we can finally revisit MGS 4 without dusting off a PlayStation 3.

Join recent Metal Gear convert Charles Harte, who will be on the sticks to experience Guns of the Patriots (via the Master Collection Vol. 2) for the very first time, alongside long-time series fan Marcus Stewart, who is revisiting MGS 4 for the first time in over a decade. The stream kicks off today live on Twitch and YouTube at 12 p.m. PT/3 p.m. ET, and will continue for two hours each week until we roll credits.

If you can't catch us live, you can watch each episode after they air by following the YouTube links below.

Every week, Game Informer editors enter the vault and dust off games from every genre and platform imaginable. Watch Replay to relive fond (and not so fond) memories from gaming’s past.

#4104. Zenelss Zone Zero Version 2.6 has you playing as an event planner and social media manager for an idol group

Zenelss Zone Zero's Encore for an Old Dream has a good excuse for introducing some new mechanics to the action game.

Zenless Zone Zero’s latest Special Program has delivered a tonne of information about the game’s big upcoming update, Version 2.6. This latest addition kicks off celebrations in New Eridu, and it’s dubbed Encore for an Old Dream.

Version 2.6 is not far off, either, arriving in ZZZ on February 6 - exactly one week from today. Encore for an Old Dream is something of an in-between story that takes place after the end of Season 2.

The narrative of 2.6 sees the Proxies’ return to Sixth Street for New Eridu's annual Gilded Carrot Day. At the centre of the celebrations is the debut of idol group Angels of Delusion at the 404 Error music venue, but not all is as it seems.

The story follows the Proxies getting invited backstage to support the group, which also includes helping them set up practice schedules, organise events and manage social media activities. There’s a rhythm minigame as part of that, along with new maps and mechanics for Marcel Adventure.

Angels of Delusion is also the group that the two new Agents being introduced in this update belong to. Members of the same group are capable of performing coordinated attacks. The new arrivals are Sunna and Aria.

Sunna is a an S-Rank Physical Support Agent who specialises in boosting teammates using Attack and Anomaly. Her Ultimate sees her pull out a giant hammer to land heavy damage, and bring teammates into combat using Quick Assist. Sunna’s companion, Bubblegum, can cast Cat's Gaze on enemies, marking them for detonation. Bubblegum can also buff the squad’s attack.

Aria is the other new arrival, the group’s lead vocalist who can shift between two forms, idol projection and construct. Aria is an Ether Anomaly Agent who also deals high burst damage, specifically against enemies who suffer from any Attribute Anomalies.

Sunna and Aria also benefit from the support of the amusingly named Bangboo Biggest Fan, a fan club president who can heal them over time, and boost the squad’s Attack any time two or more Angels of Delusion members are present.

Version 2.6’s S-Rank re-runs are Yixuan (Auric Ink - Rupture), and Yuzuha (Physical - Support), who you can look forward to as part of the banners.

Version 2.6 will also expand Hollow Zero with a new game mode, Operation Matrix. The mode offers themed stages that rotate weekly, each offering new mechanics. You can now also Sweep in Hollow Zero.

Beyond all the celebrations, this update also brings combat kit overhauls to a couple of older S-Rank characters, Lycaon and Harumasa. You can look forward to multiple limited-time events, too, including one where you can earn a new outfit for Pan Yinhu.

The big event is naturally going to be themed around Gilded Carrot Day, and it actually starts today. There’s the usual run of login rewards (about 3,300 Polychromes), as well as daily activities. Yet another login event - Gilded Surprise, Wonderful Boo-ns - will be available February 14-23, offering daily draws from a pool of 4 billion Polychrome.

As always, there’s no reason not to catch up on the latest set of Zenless Zone Zero codes for some free in-game items.

#4103. Tom Holland Might Be Starring in Another Naughty Dog Movie Adaptation

Greg has more than than 10 years of experience in video game journalism, covering some of the biggest games on the 8th and 9th generations of console.

It seems that Naughty Dog can’t get enough of Tom Holland, after he starred in their blockbuster live-action Uncharted adaptation. Appearing as Nathan Drake, Holland was a hit with fans and casuals and the film raked in over $400 million at the global box office.

Now, the studio appears to have tapped Holland again to star in the next installment in their cinematic universe, with a new report placing the English actor as signed on for the much-rumored project.

Which top-tier PlayStation 2 game series never left the comforts of the platform?

A new report through Production Weekly indicates that Holland is attached to a Jak & Daxter adaptation, a film which he has expressed a personal desire to appear in in the past. His name appears under the cast section, with the film being directed by Ruben Fleischer, who helmed Naughty Dog’s previous Uncharted adaptation.

The Production Weekly issue is from June 2025 but was recently unearthed by fans, and appears to be reputable, as it connects with a previous report from the same time that A Minecraft Movie writers Neil Widener and Gavin James had signed on to write the screenplay. Production Weekly is a long-running trade newsletter that tracks upcoming film and television productions, including details on projects in development, pre-production, and active filming.

[Holland’s] name appears under the cast section, with the film being directed by Ruben Fleischer, who helmed Naughty Dog’s previous Uncharted adaptation.

The project was set for a tentative 2026 shooting date, being filmed in London by Sony Pictures Entertainment. A synopsis of the movie reads: “After Daxter falls into a Dark Eco silo at the forbidden Misty Island, he is transformed from a human into an ottsel, a fictional hybrid of an otter and weasel. In a quest to return Daxter to human form, he and Jak set out to find the Dark Eco sage Gol Acheron. However, the duo find Acheron corrupted by Dark Eco, choosing to use the elusive Light Eco to defeat him and save the world at the cost of Daxter remaining in his ottsel form.”

Holland himself has previously expressed that he’d love to play Jak in any planned adaptation, saying in 2022: "I would like to make a Jak and Daxter movie, and I would play Jak... But I would make it A24, so it was really weird and dark. Yeah, I would do a really weird live-action version of Jak and Daxter." No details about the film except the synopsis are available, or whether it'll be as dark as Holland hopes.

A live-action Jak & Daxter adaptation would be the first time the franchise has made it to the silver screen, and would certainly breathe new life into Naughty Dog’s dormant IP, which hasn’t seen any new games since 2009’s Jak and Daxter: The Lost Frontier on PlayStation Portable. Despite the huge gap between releases, the franchise is still a cult classic and has a legion of dedicated fans—with Naughty Dog surely feeling another box office success starring Holland would be a great way to attract a new generation of players to their iconic duo.

Despite the huge gap between releases, the franchise is still a cult classic and has a legion of dedicated fans.

Some players believe that the film may come alongside a major remake of Jak & Daxter’s original outing, which launched in 2001 on PlayStation 2. It would certainly follow the ongoing trend of studios remaking their classic titles for modern audiences, and would indicate a back to basics move for Naughty Dog after its major successes with Uncharted and The Last of Us franchises.

Whether Naughty Dog is willing to invest that much time and money in reviving a series still remains unknown, but it would certainly push the 3D platformer back into the public eye and hopefully mirror successes of other PlayStation classics that made the jump to modern consoles, like Spyro The Dragon and Ratchet and Clank.

Intergalactic: The Heretic Prophet, the upcoming Naughty Dog game, is reportedly in the final stages of production.

#4102. The Video Games And More You Should Play This Weekend – November 13, 2026

Today is Friday the 13th, but let's not dwell on that. Here are some weekend video games to play. Well, actually, here are some of our biggest stories of the week, and then you can check out some weekend game recommendations.

Also, go ahead and make some space on your Xbox or PlayStation hard drive to make room for GTAVI. It's going to be about 200 GB and you can pre-load it now. Delete those games you're not going to return to. Delete all those video clips you'll never watch from every time you get a Trophy on your PlayStation. And you know what? Go ahead and delete Fortnite, too. It's time.

Calling all sickos of The Rootrees Are Dead, Return of the Obra Dinn, The Incident At Galley House, and everything in between: there’s another good deduction game to obsess over. Funeral for the Sun stars a historian who visits an abandoned Latin American town to piece together its turbulent history, chiefly the truth behind the mysterious disappearance of its hundreds of residents (who were, officially speaking, lost in a fire). Supernatural forces allow players to peer into the town’s past to learn about key people potentially responsible for the calamity, who they must identify by name, establish relationships between, and even match younger and older versions of themselves. You even keep track of information using a multi-function notebook à la The Roottrees Are Dead. Boasting an enticing story, a beautiful painterly art direction, and a tight runtime at roughly 8-hours (or less if you’re really on a roll), Funeral for the Sun is a mystery worth unraveling if you need a new deduction game to cozy up with.

NetEase has continued to impress with the pace and quality of its regular updates to Marvel Rivals, which continues today with the release of an 11th season for the superhero battler. Right here at launch, the notable addition is he arrival of X-Men hero Nightcrawler, who BAMFs his way into battle as a strategist, equally capable of healing allies and taking out foes with his sword and brimstone bombs. As is almost always the case right at a new hero’s launch, it can be hard to snag him on the roster on opening day to see how he plays, but once you do, I expect you’ll find him a versatile healer who can pretty dramatically shake up the battlefield, especially with his Ultimate, which basically consolidates allies and enemies together in one central clump for a frenzied exchange of blows. Alongside the new batch of seasonal cosmetics and events to dive into, it’s once again a good time to don your hero outfit and take on some matches.

Pikmin 4 released on Switch 2 this week (or upgraded to Switch 2 depending on how you look at it), and that's a good thing. Pikmin 4 is the best game in the series and the Switch 2 version is the best version. That's great for those who never finished the game (your save does transfer) or skipped Pikmin 4 when it released in 2023, but if you're looking for an excuse to return to the game and play new content, the Dandori Academy addition is underwhelming. You can read my full thoughts here.

Metaphor: ReFantazio, originally released in 2024, is a great RPG from the creators of Persona. And the Persona lineage is obvious throughout the full game. You have to pick and choose where and with whom you should be spending your time, all while a big world-saving RPG with a memorable party of characters plays out in the foreground.

It released this week for Switch 2 and it’s a game that I think would play well on a handheld device. It’s also just a good RPG to play if you missed it previously.

Fun fact: Metaphor: ReFantazio was the game we had lined up to be the next cover when we were temporarily shut down in in 2024. We went to the studio and had a cover drawn up and everything. You can read the full details of the cover story that never was right here.

You can also read Game Informer's review of Metaphor: ReFantazio by following the link.

As we enjoy the final week in a pre-GTA VI world, what better way to gird your loins for next week’s release, so to speak, than by revisiting the last adventures set in Rockstar’s take on Miami? 2002’s Grand Theft Auto: Vice City is a certified classic that, if you’ve never played it, offers nice foundational insight into what Vice City was like in the ’80s (spoiler: it was a lot like Scarface and Miami Vice). Best of all, Vice City is easily available on current platforms with modernized improvements to boot.

If you want to go even further back, chronologically speaking, Grand Theft Auto: Vice City Stories is a prequel set two years before the events of Vice City. Maybe, in some extremely minute way, Vice City Stories lays narrative groundwork for GTA VI. It’s unlikely, but you never know. Originally released for PSP in 2006, Vice City Stories is trickier to play if you don’t own Sony's retired handheld or a PlayStation 2, which it was ported to in 2007. But if you can find the means, there’s no better time to check out this often overlooked chapter of Vice City’s history.

I usually hold off on early access games, to preserve my experience for the finished product, but I just couldn’t resist Slay the Spire 2. The co-op gameplay is an awesome, major change, but even just adding a couple of new characters and cards would have satisfied my cravings. To that end, this week’s free update adds a brand new character, the Fool, who I’m eager to test out.

FYI, this new character is only available on the game’s beta, so you’ll have to go into the game settings on steam, click Properties, then Game Versions & Betas, and then opt into the “public-beta” version of the game to check the new content out. The patch notes for this update specifically say, “We expect to make a great number of content and balance changes before the Fool is ready for the main branch,” so expect frequent tweaks and a bit of a wait before the Fool joins the main Early Access branch. The new beta update also adds two more game modes: Dread and Blitz, which drastically alter your runs. If you want to wait a little while, the team at Mega Crit will refine these options into a more final form. But if you’re like me, more Slay the Spire 2 is more Slay the Spire 2, and I’m hopping in as soon as I can.

Monster Train 2 was one of my favorite games of last year, so I’m always glad to have a reason to jump back in. This week’s DLC, The Punished, is a perfect opportunity to do so, adding a new clan to the base game’s already packed roster. Since any clan can be combined with a second one to start a run, adding just one more option at the game’s start has an exponential effect, expanding the ways you can approach each attempt. As the DLC’s name implies, the new Punished clan gains buffs when taking damage, and you get new suite of cards that damages the whole playing field at once, harming foes and bolstering your allies. Even if you’re not checking out the DLC, the base game is absolutely worth picking up – just read my glowing review.

If you’ve been hankering for a new direction to go with your tabletop RPG group, may I recommend the incredibly versatile Cypher System from Monte Cook Games? The new Character Rulebook includes everything you need to get started, and set your adventures in virtually any fictional backdrop you can imagine, from hard sci-fi to gritty horror to high fantasy. Cypher’s polished approach to narrative-first and player-focused game sessions is much easier to pick up than many new rules systems, but it has enormous flexibility to deliver smart, creative, and exciting adventures that can help to change things up if your playing group has been in a rut.

#4101. Starsand Island is a life and farming sim that isn't gacha, and it's out next week

Starsand Island officially has an Early Access release date, and it sounds like it won't stay there for years.

Though it may seem like we just had a big life sim release in Heartopia, 2026 actually has more than one highly-anticipated release in that particular subgenre of cozy game. The next big one on the horizon is Starsand Island, the life and farming sim from Seed Sparkle Lab.

The game has been gaining momentum since the launch of a demo in October last year, but the developer never quite managed to commit to a date for its debut title. Until now.

Seed Sparkle Lab announced today that Starsand Island will enter Early Access on February 11, which is only a bit over one week from now. This goes for Steam and the Xbox Preview Program version.

The developer said to expect a fairly short Early Access run, as the full launch is expected in the summer of this year. When the full release arrives, the game will also make the jump to PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series, as well as Switch 2.

The full release is also expected to bring Steam Deck support and introduce the multiplayer mode, which will not be available during Early Access

Starsand Island has something of a unique look compared to other games in the subgenre. The storybook, anime-inspired aesthetics are popular in the realm of gacha games, of course. However, seeing as this particular game isn’t gacha, being a premium product means it’s going to offer something free-to-play games aren’t designed to.

Speaking of which, the game will be available in two editions: Standard and Deluxe, with the latter including Romanticism-inspired outfits, furniture, and other customisation items. If you buy either during launch, you’ll also get a Chinese New Year bonus with even more outfits and furniture.

On top of the usual systems of farming, mining, and making friends with adorable characters (and animals), the game also has combat that pits you against ancient guardians. You can, of course, also build a home in it, and decorate it to your heart's content.

Seed Sparkle Lab says you can expect about 100 hours of content in the Early Access launch build, and more features will arrive over the course of the next six or so months, including a crossover event with My Time At Portia.

You can look forward to more Starsand Island coverage from us in the near future. Until then, you can get started by planning who you’re going to date now.

#4100. PS5 Exclusive Destruction AllStars Shuts Down On November 25

PlayStation embarked on a live service push a few years ago, and there’s a trail of bodies lying in its wake, most of which never even saw the light of day. Destruction AllStars did make it out alive, but only just. The PS5 exclusive hasn’t been available to buy for a while, and from November 25, it will no longer be playable at all, barring one unsupported feature.

In May of 2026, PlayStation delisted Destruction AllStars along with the game’s virtual currency. It gave those who still play the game a little more time to keep playing offline, with the promise that it will end service on November 25, 2026.

At the time of writing this, that date is tomorrow, which means if you have continued to play Destruction AllStars offline, your fun is about to forcibly come to an end. Server support will officially be shut down at 3 pm UTC on November 25. That’s 10 am EST, so technically you will still be able to play for a little while tomorrow too.

Be sure to download these dozens of digital exclusive PS3 titles before they're gone for good when the PS3 digital storefront closes.

You might actually still be able to play after that time has passed, as PlayStation’s shutdown statement clarifies that the game’s single-player arcade challenges might still be available. Emphasis on the “might”, as with support for the game being pulled entirely, if something were to immediately break, which seems likely, there will be no one on the other end to fix it.

If you have any of that aforementioned virtual currency left, now is the time to spend it. Once Destruction AllStars is shut down, that money will simply disappear. If you do still have any left over, you have effectively already lost it since anything you buy today will be gone by tomorrow.

Destruction AllStars managed to avoid the live service grim reaper for five years, although that is giving the game a lot of credit it definitely does not deserve. When PlayStation announced it would be shutting down the game and ended multiplayer service effective immediately, it had basically been broken for two years.

The same statement that confirmed the game’s shutdown noted that multiplayer services would remain offline indefinitely due to “ongoing technical issues”. It remains unclear, and may stay that way forever, whether PlayStation was actively trying to fix the problems for all that time and couldn’t figure it out, or it simply didn’t care due to lack of player interest and eventually let everyone know that it wasn’t even trying to fix things behind the scenes.

Destruction AllStars will be a relatively small footnote when gaming historians inevitably write about PlayStation’s infamously poor live service push. Concord’s cancelation and Naughty Dog being forced to waste time and resources on a game that would never be released, The Last of Us Online, will be the focus. It’s a footnote all the same, though, and had it been a more notable release, its immediate failure might have forced PlayStation to rethink this whole live service thing before it led to layoffs and studio closures.

Sony's refusal to change course has been further highlighted as new PS5 boxes warn about 2028 changes.
