#4071. 9 Best Tech Parodies in GTA 6

Aden Carter is a Contributor at DualShockers who has been covering games professionally since 2020. He specializes in lists and guides, with a focus on RPGs, horror games, survival horror, Soulslikes, cozy/sim games, and action-adventure titles. Before joining DualShockers, Aden contributed to GameRant, XDA, Gamepur, I

The Grand Theft Auto series tends to be a parody of real life, with there being loads of satirical comedy woven throughout the many fibers of each game. This trend continues in Grand Theft Auto 6, with there being loads of hilarious parodies of well-known companies, television shows, radio broadcasts, and even tech.

Tech plays a big role in the game, as you use your phone for many things, such as ordering a ride on the RydeMe app, or even bucking yourself using the aptly named BuckMe app.

You are going to be relying on a lot of tech companies throughout GTA 6, so it is obvious that there will be a number of jokes surrounding them.

Texting plays a huge role in real life. After all, you text your friends, family members, and even coworkers about what is going on in your life. The same is done in GTA 6, and the game captures texting quite well, with both protagonists texting one another and various people about jobs.

While you may normally use the popular WhatsApp application to get your fill of communication, the people of GTA 6 use a slightly different app called WhatUp. This is a very obvious parody of WhatsApp, with a name that is almost identical.

Even the user interface is almost identical, with it featuring a very minimalist style showing the avatar or profile picture of each contact next to the messages.

Amazon is a go-to tech and shipping company for many people nowadays. While we all may complain about capitalism, there is no denying the convenience of having everything at your fingertips through the use of an app that has next-day shipping.

In GTA, the citizens of Leonida are using a slightly different company that is a clear parody of Amazon, and it is called Sahara. You can find boxes scattered around that mimic the exact shipping tape used by the company, the logo is very similar, and there is even Sahara Mirage, which is meant to be a parody of Amazon Prime.

Money makes the world go ‘round in real life, and it especially makes the world go ‘round in GTA 6. You are on a constant mission to collect money in the game, which in a way mimics real life. Anyway when you are handling money in real life, you might use a banking app, or you might use CashApp or Venmo.

GTA 6 has an app that parodies these real-life tools and it is called BuckMe - a hilarious name that has various uses, such as when you give yourself money, which is called bucking yourself.

This app is the go-to banking app that you get at the start of the game because you can’t afford to open a real checking account and it is just perfect.

In typical Rockstar fashion, get ready for some parodies of popular websites and mobile apps.

Did you know that you can play games within GTA 6? Odds are you probably did, and it is thanks to Cal. He so graciously installs the new JoyStation in Jason’s home early in the game, allowing you to catch up on your gaming within your game.

The JoyStation is an obvious parody of the PlayStation 5, with the console looking almost identical to the real-life system you are probably playing GTA 6 on. Even the user interface looks extremely close to the real-life version.

The console isn’t just for looks, as it can be used to play some real games, with some of them even being easter eggs for real-life movies and games.

When you need to get around the city in real life, you either rely on your car to get you from point A to point B, or you rely on someone else’s car. This can come in the form of a ride that you hire via a rideshare app like Lyft or Uber.

Just like in real life, you can get from point to point in GTA 6 by using the convenient ridesharing app aptly called RydeMe. It even comes complete with a Y instead of an I so you know it was made by the tech bros in Silicon Valley.

The app is great, as it lets you fast travel around the city. If only you could skip the unwanted conversation with the driver in real life. At least the prices match up with the inflated real-life equivalent.

A new Grand Theft Auto 6 leak has finally shown Lucia's gameplay and opening chapter, confirming that Uber/Lyft parodies are in the game.

Doomscrolling has become the norm lately, as apps like YouTube, Instagram, and TikTok all offer short-form content that you can easily digest and swipe away. Luckily, GTA 6 hasn’t gone that far… yet.

While you can’t doomscroll reels in GTA 6, you can flip through tons of posts thanks to the improved Snapmatic app. This app made an appearance in GTA 5, as it was used to take pictures.

Now, you can use it to scroll through countless posts about how we got something else before RAC 7. You can even read the comments, and those are something else entirely, so be prepared.

Dating in real life has been boiled down to a few different dating apps, but if you are looking to hook up with someone, you are probably going to use Tinder. Of course, you could try FarmersOnly, but to each their own.

Sadly, you can’t get the experience of using a dating app in GTA 6, but you can help out Cal. Early in the game, you get to see the in-game version of Tinder, as Cal hands you his phone and you get to swipe right or left on various dating profiles.

The app is pretty accurate to the real-life equivalent, complete with cringy profiles, horrible pictures, and people with way too high of standards.

There has been a rise of people who are vaping, and as someone who used to vape all the time, it is sad to see how much it has grown at times. Vaping has infected the world of Leonida as well, but one in particular that is worth pointing out is Manifestick.

This hilarious parody is meant to replace anxiety pens and mock those who wear a vape on a leash around their neck, as there are women who use them like they are addicted to them.

Oh wait, that is because they are addicted. You can discover that these vape pens are laced with cocaine, making them not so friendly and very addictive like the real-life nicotine infused sticks.

Cryptocurrency is everywhere nowadays. There are people who swear on Bitcoin, and we see a meme coin pop up almost every day. We have all heard stories of people being scammed because someone did a rug pull.

Throughout the game, you will interact with a company called AudaCity, and there is even a character named Papa Audacity. This company is creating DacityCoin, and you are meant to promote it with Redbull-style stunts that push the coin’s value up.

The protagonists even call out how the coin is a scam, but that doesn’t mean you can’t get in on the ground floor and be one of the few who profits off of everyone else’s losses.

Like many games, Grand Theft Auto 6 is full of easter eggs for you to discover. These are some of the best Leonida has to offer.

#4070. You're not crazy, trying to heal in Nioh 3 sometimes doesn't work - and Team Ninja is fixing it

One of the more insidiously aggravating bugs in Nioh 3 makes it so the game ignores you when you try to use elixirs, but hopefully not for long.

Nioh 3 has received a hot new update that brings plenty of bug fixes to very specific issues, but it also implements fixes for a few of the most common - and incredibly annoying - bugs. Patch 1.03.01 arrived earlier on all platforms, and it comes with a chunky set of notes.

This latest update, predictably, doesn’t add any gameplay features, but some of the included fixes will absolutely delight - or vindicate - so many of the game’s millions of players.

There’s plenty to go through in the patch notes published today for update 1.03.01, but the most impactful is a fix for an issue that “sometimes made it impossible to use elixirs during battle.” This is only a partial fix, but if you ran into the problem of smashing that shortcut button and not seeing your character play the healing animation, you’ll be glad to see it.

This is a problem myself and others have faced, especially in boss fights. You can even see the shortcut register your button press and proceed to ignore you. Another partial fix has been made to an issue that caused the game to crash. Team Ninja didn’t share specifics on that, and though Nioh 3 has been fairly stable for me in 70+ hours, it has definitely crashed a few times.

If you’ve been playing since launch, you likely have - or know someone who has - run into issues with save file corruption and other weird bugs around certain trackable items within save files.

Team Ninja already rolled out a couple of fixes there, and this latest one specifically targets losing valuables during Myths. If your save file has been affected, the game will now check and recover what was lost. Even more interesting is that the game will now automatically create a backup copy of your save data any time you load a save.

If you’ve made it into the Eternal Rift, you’ll be happy to know that today’s update takes care of a few progression blockers, and fixes an issue that allowed some players to obtain certain items before they were supposed to, locking themselves out.

One of the more amusing fixes concerns Mujina, who had a tendency to respawn if you prayed at a Shrine after opening a chest it was hiding in, which made it appear far more often than a mimic should.

Finally, there’s a set of fixes that address bugs (and exploits) when using specific Martial Art with certain weapons. There are a few fixes to AI, Myths, and one problem with the Minamoto no Yoritomo boss fight that made it impossible to interrupt him, even after he runs out of Ki.

Hit the link at the top for the full change log, and check out our Nioh 3 gameplay tips if you haven’t already. You should also change these settings ASAP, as they’re going to make your life much easier and save you a lot of time.

#4069. Grand Theft Auto VI Review - Outrageous Fortune

Many superlatives will be heard in the discussion around Grand Theft Auto VI – biggest world, most activities, best graphics, deepest narrative – but its real triumph is the way all those features and others work in service of a cohesive, believable immersion in a criminal fantasy that is hard to grasp until you’ve played it for yourself.

Rockstar’s latest returns players to a dramatically expanded version of the Vice City seen in a prior game, now largely unrecognizable after real and in-game years have passed. Leonida is a joy to explore, filled with a wealth of activities, both mundane and illicit. The game’s design makes many ordinary tasks as compelling as the illegal ones. Go fishing off the boat, brew coffee to wake up, work out at the gym, scuba dive for long-lost treasure, dust crops, motocross in the mud, go dancing at the club. As you move between those activities, the world feels alive with minor events, from traffic accidents to shady individuals a little too interested in your walk to the ATM. GTAVI delights in life's minutiae, with animations, voice lines, and background characters that keep things fresh even dozens of hours into the story. The level of detail everywhere is astounding and, at times, overwhelming. Getting sidetracked is easy.

The focus on detail carries into the visuals. Lucia’s hair blows in the wind, and she absently pushes it back behind her ear. A drug den is littered with paraphernalia and empty containers. A shifty contact quirks a smile – your only hint that things are about to go south. Sweat glistens on your character’s skin after a hard workout, their breathing and heart rate noticeably heightened. Clouds roll together in the sky, creating realistic weather simulations. The commitment to an authentic simulated world is encompassing, thoughtful, and intentional, a testament to hand-crafted and meticulously painstaking development work, paying off in an absorbing play-space that is hard to step away from.

While the day-to-day simulation is fascinating, it also adds pacing and counterpoint to the explosive march of major missions, narrative threads, and set-piece encounters that drive the game forward. Not even one of these meticulously choreographed sequences deserves to be spoiled; they run the gamut from amusing shenanigans at a strip club to intense chases and escapes fueled by raging gunfights and explosions. Many of the best moments leverage an expert sense of musical accompaniment, weaving a slick original score alongside one of the most impressive and wide-ranging licensed soundtracks ever heard in a video game – often to surprisingly emotional effect.

Ranged combat is punchy and enjoyable; smart use of cover and time-slowing focus makes most battles manageable. On-foot navigation is in a similar boat – simple to pick up and uninterested in needless complexity or challenge; the focus is on choosing smart moments for stealth, knowing when to run and when to fight, and selecting the precise instant for a burst of sudden action. Driving is fast and intense, made more appealing by a huge variety of functionally distinct vehicles to enjoy. If there’s a fault to the core and optional story missions, it’s that many feel a bit on rails regarding where to go and what to do at each step. At the same time, that directed approach keeps the pace relentless, and the action and outcomes thrilling. Over many hours, the game morphs and throws new wrenches into the mix at key junctures, teasing and then playing out criminal experiences from petty theft to group heists to illicit spec ops, and punctuates those distinct vibes with memorable and singular moments.

Like its predecessors, GTAVI simultaneously lampoons and celebrates life in modern America, taking aim at targets like social media, wellness lifestyles, rap and music culture, manosphere content, and dozens more. The caricatures land so well because, in many cases, they’re (sadly) barely over the line of the absurdity we see reflected in real life, and because Rockstar so ably captures individual subcultures, dialects, and situations. Behind it all is a scathing critique of wealth inequality and the inherent unfairness of a system that sets most up to fail. It’s a bitter message delivered in honey-wrapped, exhilarating gameplay, but it shines through.

Of all its significant feats, the relationship between Lucia and Jason elevates the game to new heights, lending this installment a heart, tension, and emotional core missing from prior entries. This is, without a doubt, video gaming’s most richly drawn and compelling romance, featuring two leads who are immediately relatable and compelling to watch. Player actions dictate the strength of their bond, deepening the sense of engagement. Like the best crime fiction, you’re left surprised by how much you cheer for two people who regularly commit terrible acts. The two collectively suffer the slings and arrows of a world that always seems stacked against them; the fortune they amass is not a power grab, but a desperate attempt to cling to each other and come out the other side together, and the player can’t help but cheer them on and dread how fate might stand in the way.

Grand Theft Auto VI is a generational game that stands toe-to-toe with many of the great crime stories and satires across other media. It showcases both the entertainment value of interactive play and the current high-water mark for technical and artistic detail in games. Hunt for and count up all the minor faults or foibles you like, but then note how you just spent another hour lost in this remarkable escape into criminality, wanton violence, egregious sex, and the elusive potential of true love.

Alex Van Aken contributed to this article.

#4068. Genshin Impact Luna 5 takes the squad back to Mondstadt, finally makes Varka playable

Genshin Impact's next update will have you reminiscing about the good ol' days of... 2020.

The latest big content update has been revealed for HoYoverse's breakout game, Genshin Impact. Version Luna 5, which has the unusually long and needlessly layered title — Song of the Welkin Moon: Variation - Homeward, He Who Caught the Wind — is set to arrive February 25.

This one is a bit of a nostalgia play, taking everyone back to Mondstadt, the place where you may remember taking your first steps. And, as with any good return to the ol’ hunting grounds, come familiar characters, too.

The big new arrival is Varka, who joins as a playable character for the first time. Varka, Grand Master of the Knights of Favonius, is a character whose debut has been long-awaited. He is a 5-Star Anemo Claymore wielder with a dual-wield combat style, capable of dealing two different types of Elemental damage. His addition means that there's now finally a burly 5-Star male character of each elemental type... do with that information what you will.

Varka's dual-wielding combat style allows him to deal two different types of Elemental damage at the same time. The way it works is that his Elemental Skill boosts the damage of his regular attacks, but it also converts the damage type of his right-hand claymore to match his teammates’ elements (Pyro, Hydro, Electro, or Cryo). The left-hand claymore always deals Anemo damage.

The more normal attacks you use, the more frequently he can activate a special Elemental Skill, or trigger a Charged Attack that doesn’t consume stamina. He can also rely on the Hexerei effect to trigger more instances of Elemental Skill, as well as Charged Attacks, making him a monster damage-dealer.

Varka, of course, has been a staple member of the cast, featuring in both the original story in a small cameo, as well as taking a bigger role in the recent Nod-Krai chapters. With the return to Mondstadt, his playable debut makes sense. His Story Quest will shed light on his encounter with the Wild Hunt, and the Great Wolf King of the North

The reruns for this version are going to be Flins — who will be available in the first phase of Event Wishes — as well as Skirk and Escoffier in the second phase. You can also look forward to the return of the Chronicled Wish with Mondstadt characters.

Staying on the theme of reminiscence, the big event in Luna 5 is centered around revisiting memories from the beginning of your time with Genshin Impact, and reuniting with old friends. In Echoes of Memory, you’ll witness familiar scenes that have been changed slightly, and you’ll need to use the Spotter Kamera to detect and record those differences.

The Knights of Favonius are hosting several other activities for everyone to take part in, including an event that lets you catch up with old friends over drinks which you make for them.

Outside of events, there’s a new set of Gliding and Combat Challenges. And, of course, there are new minigames that you can relax with. The Kamera is being utilised yet again, and this time you can use to capture sights from your time in spots across Natlan, Fontaine, and Sumeru. There’s also… a horde mode of a sort, where you fend off waves of enemies.

#4067. Mailbox: Ocarina Intruders, Pikmin Day, Too Many Humans - Nintendo Life Letters

Hello, you. Yes, you. It's just us here today - everyone else is busy in Hyrule or Leonida right now.

In fact, it's been like that for most of the month, it seems, as the Nintendo Life Mailbox is looking pretty empty! So, it'll be a nice quick one this month. We'll have you back with your preferred ride — equine or automotive — in a jiffy.

Got something you want to get off your chest? Remember, we're ready and waiting to read about your game-related ponderings as we head into the holidays. Each month we’ll highlight a Star Letter, the writer of which will receive a month’s subscription to our ad-free Supporter scheme. Check out the submission guidelines at the bottom of this page.

So, let's slice open our correspondence...

I've been inspired to share in this letter about my first encounter with The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time following the feature you ran on this very topic, because it's a touching, unique story.

I was about 11 years old in 1998 and had been avidly following OoT in the magazines, absorbing every screenshot and article about this sword and shield weilding greened tuniced hero.

Bizarrely I'd never played a Zelda game before but something about it looked magical and exciting. So I did what any 11 year old would do. I asked for the game for Christmas.

So, Christmas morning arrives and I excitedly tumble down the stairs to the presents under the tree. I open them all but.... There's a pang of absence. No Zelda game. Where is it I exclaim!? And my mum sheepishly informs me that it didn't arrive in time for Christmas.

I cry. Real tears. I'm distraught. Inconsolable. For months I've waited for this amazing looking game and I can't play it.

What happened next is... I think... wonderful parenting.

While I was busy in my bedroom creating my own water temple with more tears than a kingdom (see what I did there?), my mum phones every parent of my school friends she knows until she finds someone with a copy of Zelda. And eventually, she does. She creeps up to knock on my door and says "Hey, Listen! I'll take you to your friends place, he has a copy"

And so, my tears stop and off I go to watch my pal play the game and suddenly a terrible Christmas becomes a brilliant one. The game is everything I imagine it to be and more and my mate and I spend hours solving Deku Tree puzzles and gasping at Hyrule Field's majesty.

So as we all enjoy the remake of Ocarina of Time decades later, I just have one thing to say: Thanks mum. You understood the stakes and you cared enough to help me get my Zelda fix that fateful Christmas of 1998.

And ever since that day, my life has been met with the least terrible of fates: I became a huge fan of Zelda and have bought every single one since on day one - no more painful Christmas mornings! YoshiTails

That is some above-and-beyond parenting, Mrs YoshiTails! We salute you.

I'm imagining what my mum would have said to some random mother ringing her on Christmas morning, asking if their kid could come over to play a video game. I assume she would have reacted in the classic British manner: agreeing to it with bemusement while silently seething, resenting the interloper for every surrendered mince pie.

I joke! I had no friends. I did have Zelda, though. - Ed.

Community "I Think Of Her Every Time I Play It" - Your Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Memories

We seem to have sleepwalked into an era of walking simulators.

I’m not talking about artsy indie games emphasising investigation over action, but big budget AAA titles starring main “characters” who look like they’ve walked out of a Hollywood movie. There are too many humans in games and it’s stifling the medium.

Back when the mascot character was king, protagonists felt properly differentiated both aesthetically and mechanically: Mario jumps, Sonic runs, Spyro flies, Crash bangs and wallops. Of these, only Mario could be called ‘human’, and even he has about as much in common with a real plumber as Sonic does with a real hedgehog.

Vibrant colours and exaggerated movements helped make the games legible on small screens when pixels, polygons and processing power came at a premium, and this gave games a unique vibe and feel. Now that we can better render humans in all their hairy, fleshy complexity, video game aesthetics have moved from ‘cartoonish’ to ‘cinematic’, and physics have followed suit.

Thing is, if I wanted to control a human, I’d put the controller down and go for a walk. (…Maybe not a bad idea actually). We’re meandering, clunky lumps of meat who navigate the world in a most pedestrian manner. Fine for a trip to the shops. Not the most inspiring thing to control in a video game.

It should be said that the ‘mascot character’ isn’t completely dead. The House of Mario was built by pixelated protags who carry the forward the flame of the 8-bit era. The portly purported plumber is still as satisfyingly springy as ever. DK has swapped pixels for vowels but continues to dish out delightful destruction like a primate possessed. Even the new squid-kids on the block - Splatoon’s Inklings - are unashamedly ‘gamey’, slipping slickly through their own mercurial fluids.

It’s a pleasant reminder that video games let us be anything we want: a bird (Untitled Goose Game), a plane (Star Fox) or even a kickflipping train (Denshattack). With that in mind, it seems a shame to be stuck as the same humdrum human that AAA titles insist on lumbering us with.

As film studios conglomerate and cinematic universes bleed into each other, I wish video games would embrace what makes them unique rather than dissolving into the same great multimedia melange. I’ve had enough of the homogeneous Homo sapiens-centric pseudo-cinema now synonymous with AAA game development and wish that more creative energies would be put into games that actually push the mechanical possibilities of the medium.

I disagree, purely because there are just so many games of all flavours out there. If you want to be a squirrel or a crab or an insect or anything else, there's never been a better time. Big, small, there's just so much incredible variety. If AAA isn't doing it for you, the other As have got you covered.

I get the sense perhaps you're reacting to the priority of animation over gamefeel in some cases - lumpy realistic animation versus snappy response? Pushing right on the stick and a moment later a soupy animation cycle transitions into the movement you've input (as opposed to Mario or Link responding instantly, if unrealistically).

If that's the case, I agree that Nintendo's approach is my preference, whatever form of animal, vegetable or mineral you're controlling. The animation of an Assassin's Creed or a GTA is incredibly impressive, but it's interminably slow if you're coming to it with a Mario mindset. I find I have to be invested in the cinema and 'show' of those games if they're going to click. My all-time favourites tend to have much more responsive controls, though. - Ed.

When Nintendo announced Pikmin Day this year for November 1st, it seemed to me that it was met with mixed reactions. People said that saying 11/1 looks like Pikmin is a bit of a stretch, and they didn't really announce anything particularly interesting. While this is true, I found it positively delightful, specifically the second half of the direct when Fuka Koshiba was revealed to be hired by Nintendo. While their conversation was a bit awkward (as Nintendo Direct dialogue always is), I thought it was super cool that they hired her just from seeing her posts on Instagram. And I've been loving the charming shorts that they've been releasing recently. And I'm not even a big Pikmin fan!

The direct was weird, certainly unnecessary, and a bit awkward, but that's what made it amazing. It was delightfully quirky, dumb, delightful, and wholly Nintendo.

I think any rational person will have responded to the 'Pikmin Day' declaration in the same way: wut. Anyone but Nintendo would have been torn to absolute shreds.

Frankly, though, with everything else going on in the world, if Shigsy wants to claim some random day for what might be their best series, crack on. A '1' looks like a Pikmin, you say, Miyamoto-san? Sure, fine. So, Pikmin 5 announcement next November, hmm? - Ed.

"For Pokémon day next year, I want a Pok" - Scottdevine53

That's all for this month! Thanks to everyone who wrote in, whether you were featured above or not.

Got something you'd like to get off your chest? A burning question you need answered? A correction you can't contain? Follow the instructions below, then, and we look forward to rifling through your missives.

#4065. Nioh 3 is, unsurprisingly, the fastest-selling game in the series with over a million units sold

Nioh 3 has taken the Nioh franchise to new heights, delivering its biggest-ever launch.

Even before the game came out, it was pretty easy to guess that Nioh 3 would be a hit. From the word of mouth leading up to launch, to the well-received free demo, there was little chance the action RPG wasn’t going to be a major deal.

Today, publisher Koei Tecmo has announced that the game has officially passed over one million copies sold worldwide across PC, and PlayStation 5. This makes it the fastest in the Nioh franchise to reach this milestone.

As a result of this fantastic launch, Nioh 3 has now pushed overall Nioh franchise sales to be over 10 million, which includes the original Nioh as well as Nioh 2. Today’s news comes just two weeks after the game arrived on PC, and PS5.

On Steam, where it’s available on PC, it shot up the Steam charts, and immediately broke the series’ previous best peak concurrent player count record. From there, the numbers kept growing, leading up to a stellar weekend where it peaked at 88,045 concurrent players on Steam, double that of its launch day.

This now stands as the largest for any Nioh game on Steam, and though we don’t have insight into how well it’s doing on PS5 specifically, it still shows that the Nioh series continues to grow.

Nioh 3 builds on everything the two prior games established, and pushes the series into the semi-open-world realm, with several larger maps that each cover a period of time in Japan’s history. In our Nioh 3 review we called it “Team Ninja’s most accomplished action game, and the series’ most accessible.”

If you’re curious about the challenging and very rewarding action RPG, start with these gameplay tips, and don’t be shy to call upon a friend (or stranger) for help using our co-op guide.

#4064. CD Projekt Red CEO Puts Ambition Ahead of Budget in Witcher and Cyberpunk Development

Daniel is a lifelong gamer with a love for various genres and gameplay styles who enjoys exploring games and playing from various angles.

It’s no secret that Grand Theft Auto 6 was not a cheap game to make, to put very, very mildly. While Rockstar has not publicly disclosed the game’s precise internal price tag, rumors have circulated that it’s somewhere in the billions, and considering the sheer scope and complexity of the game’s world, I don’t think that theory is an unreasonable one.

Considering the amount of cash that undoubtedly went into GTA 6’s development, which has now been followed by immense success and landmark profits for Rockstar and Take-Two, also in the billions, something of a new precedent has been established for the AAA gaming sector. Arguably, it's not a great one: if you keep pouring massive stacks of cash into your game, it’ll magically make billions of dollars forever.

Obviously, this is completely untrue, but that doesn’t stop people from wondering, especially as far as other power-player devs are concerned. For example, CD Projekt Red, developer and publisher of landmark IPs like The Witcher and Cyberpunk, has invested its fair share of capital into its works. However, according to its CEO, Michal Nowakowski, the budget of CDPR’s titles is secondary to their ambitions and goals.

Rockstar is known for putting insane levels of detail into their games, but here is how they are going above and beyond with GTA VI.

During CD Projekt Red’s Q3 2026 Earnings Call, the audio of which was posted to the company’s official YouTube channel, Nowakowski was asked his opinion on the “technological and qualitative leap” between Grand Theft Auto 5 and 6, and in turn, how those landmark advancements might inform CDPR’s developmental philosophy going forward, particularly with in-development Witcher and Cyberpunk titles.

Nowakowski acknowledged the major precedent that has been put forth by Rockstar through GTA 6 through the industry at large, but he also clarified that, in spite of that game’s success, he and his company don’t make their games just to compete with those produced by another.

“If anything happened as a result of GTA 6, it's always great to see games like that because they show you how much cool stuff can be done. That's for sure an inspiration in many ways for our developers.”

He and his company don’t make their games just to compete with those produced by another.

When asked how GTA 6’s developmental scope might affect budget expectations for upcoming games, Nowakowski stressed that Witcher and Cyberpunk are not “budget-driven developments,” and while he is always conscious of how much money it costs to make top-shelf games, it’s not really conducive to a product’s health to be constantly keeping the budget in mind during the developmental process.

“They are ambition-driven developments and money is important, the budgets are not indefinite, that's not what we're saying. And honestly, that philosophy has not changed for us because of GTA 6.”

The obvious problem with expecting new games, even AAA ones, to have comparable budget and scope to GTA 6 is that not every game is GTA 6, nor is every developer Rockstar. Not everyone is going to have that kind of raw spending power available, and certainly, not everyone has access to the kind of prestige IP with a baked-in fanbase like GTA.

Overbloated budgets for AAA games have already been a consistent problem and talking point for at least a decade now, with players regularly complaining that too much money is spent on making games look visually and technologically impressive without making the core experience any better. This ends up dragging out development cycles and bleeding companies dry, not to mention subjecting developmental staff to intense crunch. Heck, lest we forget, GTA 6 took over a decade itself to come out, and was delayed twice.

While it is heartening to hear Nowakowski’s proclamation of ambition over budget, it is very difficult to predict where the AAA sector is going now that the shadow of GTA 6 is looming over it. Personally, I’d like to believe that players won’t expect every new game they play to also be GTA 6-tier, but, well…

GTA VI will be one of the biggest video game releases in our lifetimes, and it will be talked about for years to come.

#4062. The Sims 4 developer hasn't forgotten about its quality of life commitment, and is back with an update on what to expect in 2026

Maxis has offered some fresh details on its long-running mission to improve player quality of life in The Sims 4.

As the The Sims 4 continues into its second decade, the volume of new content, major expansions, and long-awaited features has grown in lockstep. Unfortunately, that has also meant that, given how old the game is, a few technical problems remain a nuisance.

The effort required to fix them is what led developer Maxis to make a commitment to improve the game’s technical state, and the developer has now returned to update the community on what to expect in 2026.

The quality of life pledge was made in September last year, through the introduction of a roadmap. Since then, the developer issued one update on its progress. Which brings us to this week’s new blog post, which further builds on everything that’s come before.

In the post, Maxis revealed a few key areas it’s going to be focusing on going forward. Though specific release dates for these changes were not shared, the list of issues should resonate with many players, as it covers many often-discussed topics.

The first stage of the new roadmap covers March through August. Over that period, you can expect Sims' autonomy to improve. This goes for things like how they choose locations for certain actions, they way they interact with certain objects, and even how often they interrupt conversations.

The infant and caregiver relationship is being updated, too, in order to improve autonomy and make sure your little Sims don’t miss out on milestones and interactions. That stage of the roadmap also includes fixes for black photo issues, and other crashes and freezing.

The next period takes place September through December, and it includes more interesting changes. One of the goals with this one is to improve Sims’ dining experience, which covers issues around eating and drinking.

Another important area of focus with this stage is family trees, and relationships between members of the same family. Maxis wants to improve the game’s genealogy systems to make relationship tracking across generations more robust so that your family history isn’t lost.

Depending on how the first stage goes, you might see more issues join the list of what the developer is looking at for the second stage of the roadmap.

The good news is that you won’t have to wait too long for the game’s next patch. Due out in March, this next update will feature around 55 fixes, including for some commonly reported issues.

Until then, you may want to check out The Sims 4’s Lost Legacies Event, which is available now until the middle of March. If you picked up the game’s latest expansion, check if you tried those Royalty & Legacy cheats.

#4061. Feature: A Lost Box Restored My Faith In Zelda's Staying Power

A few weeks ago, my brother sent me a photo with zero context. He was at our parents’ house, helping them pack up for a cross-country move, when he found something unusual: a heavy metal box with a latch.

It took me a second to dust off the cobwebs in that corner of my mind, but once I did, I recognised the box as the promotional material Nintendo sent me back in 1998 to celebrate the original release of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.

I asked my bro what was inside the box and a few moments later he replied with another picture. The box was empty.

I can’t think of anything more depressing than an empty treasure chest. All the anticipation leading to… crushing disappointment. Anyone who ever slogged through the Phoenix Cave in Final Fantasy VI knows the feeling.

This chest originally housed a pre-launch, gold N64 cart of Ocarina of Time. It was Nintendo’s not-so-subtle message that this game was a treasure. A bit on the nose, but the zeitgeist of an entire generation of gamers has certainly proven them right. OoT is a treasure.

In this case, I can at least take solace knowing that I'm the one who emptied the chest and thoroughly enjoyed its golden treasure. The empty box is evidence of that.

My brother’s timing was impeccable — bordering on eerie — unearthing the box less than a week before the Switch 2 remake launched.

Like many of you, my son (let's call him Tim) and I were eagerly awaiting the OoT remake. He hadn’t played the original, but is an avid Zelda fan, particularly the modern titles. I knew I’d love the Remake, but I was a bit nervous that he would have a different reaction. He’s a member of this Breath of the Wild, open-world generation, after all. Would the old-school Zelda formula appeal to his generation, or would it die with mine?

As they say, sometimes one man’s treasure is another man’s trash.

My love for Zelda, and desire to pass it down to my son, parallels the experience my father had with his four boys. Dad loved to work with his hands and my brothers and I were always enlisted in projects: everything from clearing the land, felling trees, reroofing the house, building an addition, repainting, and working on a long series of rundown cars. He made sure we received hands-on working experience.

Right around the time I received the Zelda Treasure Chest, my dad began restoring classic Ford Mustangs in his garage. I had already moved out, but my youngest brother ( the one who found the chest) was there to be Dad’s understudy. Together they restored two beautiful Mustangs, allowing my dad to share his love for mechanical craft and manual labour.

Sharing an old classic is one thing, but actually passing down a passion depends on how well the original holds up to modern sensibilities.

A restored car regains its iconic look, but it will also retain the old feel, complete with stiff brakes and crank windows. After all, restoring something doesn’t place it in a state opposite to its nature. A 1967 Mustang GT Fastback is a 1967 Mustang GT Fastback only if it looks, sounds, and feels like a 1967 Mustang GT Fastback, for better or worse.

Media remakes and remasters are often criticised for following this type of approach. Shot-for-shot remakes come across as unnecessary cash grabs (looking at you Disney) while complete reimaginings seem to either spectacularly succeed (Dune, Casino Royale, Metroid Zero Mission) or fail (Planet of the Apes 2001, Secret of Mana, Quantum Leap).

Like my old man, Nintendo’s philosophy seems closer to restoration than reimagining. Star Fox and Super Mario RPG are recent examples, with the slightly more ambitious Link’s Awakening preceding them by a few years. There are many others.

In each case, the spirit of the original is preserved while a few quality-of-life improvements are added. And of course, each old classic receives a new coat of paint.

By taking this approach, Nintendo has been careful to avoid the pitfalls that so many media companies encounter when updating beloved products. Their roster of remakes have largely avoided any 'Han shot first' controversies. Thank goodness.

A philosophy of preserving the original’s frame, while souping up the engine, allows old and new players to enjoy the gaming experience without fighting retro clunkiness.

So, what does Tim think of Ocarina of Time?

He loves it, of course! And it’s been immensely satisfying to see him enjoy it. Confirmation bias can be a wonderful thing.

The wife and I have a ritual of playing Zelda games together, so we’re playing it in short, infrequent bursts. I’m not complaining, as it’s allowed me to savour the experience. Tim, on the other hand, is powering through it at a much faster pace. He also spectates while my wife and I play. We always aim for a 100% run, so Tim takes notes on all of the heart pieces and bag upgrades he missed.

I’m just excited to see my son enjoying a game I grew up with. My dad passed on his love for mechanical craft to his boys, and I’m sharing my passion for sidequests with mine.

It’s been a good month. It began with a nostalgic relic and a bit of disappointment (grr, I still can’t find that gold cart), but also included a timeless masterpiece that’s been successfully passed to the next generation.

30 years ago my dad shared the muscle cars from his youth. This year I got to share a classic Zelda adventure from mine.

I wonder what treasure my boy will pass on to his kids in 30 years' time.

Have you successfully passed a favourite game down to the next generation? Was it the original, or a remake that added modern improvements? Share your stories in the comments below.
